chunks: From him, from Ayyub ibn Nuha, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mansur Buruj, from Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him), who said:

I said: A man from your mawali married a woman, then divorced her, and she became independent from him. He wanted to remarry her, but she refused him except that he make a vow to God that he would not divorce her and would not marry another woman over her. He gave her that, then it occurred to him to marry another woman after that. So what should he do?

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Bad is what he did, and how could he know what would occur in his heart by night and by day? Tell him to fulfill the condition for the woman, for indeed the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The believers are bound by their conditions.''

And there is no contradiction between this narration and the first one, because this narration is based on a type of recommendation (istihbab), for whoever has the description contained in the report is recommended to fulfill what he pledged with his tongue, so he does not contradict it, even if it is not obligatory. On this narration, what it contained is that he made it for God, and this is a vow (nadh) that became obligatory for him to fulfill. And what preceded in the first narration is that they made it upon themselves, and he did not say 'for God', so it was not a vow obligatory to fulfill, and he was free to choose in that matter. Thus the two hadiths differ. And this does not contradict the hadith we previously mentioned from Hammada, sister of Abu Ubaydah al-Hadda', that Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) invalidated the condition of one who says at the time of marriage: 'I will not marry another woman over you,' because that narration contains that he said that to her, and it was her dowry (mahr). And this is permissible. Do you not see that he said in the report: 'And she (the woman) was pleased,' meaning the woman, that that was her dowry? And the report we mentioned contained that if he made it a vow to God, it is not that it becomes her dowry, so it was obligatory for him to fulfill it. And when each of the two spouses swears that he will not marry over the other, not in the manner of a vow, it is not obligatory for him to fulfill it, and he is free to choose. Narrated.

key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابُ: Recommendation (istihbab), a recommended but not obligatory act
key_terms.الْمُؤْمِنُونَ عِنْدَ شُرُوطِهِمْ: The believers are bound by their conditions (Prophetic hadith)
key_terms.مَهْرًا: Dowry (mahr), the payment given to the wife
key_terms.مَوَالِيكَ: Your freedmen/clients (mawali), referring to the man's dependents
key_terms.نَذْرٌ: Vow (nadh), a pledge made to God that becomes obligatory to fulfill

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a vow to God and a personal marital condition in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this narration by distinguishing between a vow made specifically to God (nadh), which carries obligatory weight, and a personal pledge, which is merely recommended (istihbab). He resolves apparent contradictions with other hadiths by clarifying that the obligation to fulfill conditions depends on whether the stipulation was framed as a vow to God or a contractual term, thereby refining the Shia jurisprudence of marital vows.
